S-AI-WorldModel addresses this question through an explicit canonical representation, regulated update dynamics, computable commitment conditions, and a source-only symbolic reconstruction pipeline. Methods. S-AI-WorldModel is the tenth architectural instantiation of the Sparse Artificial Intelligence paradigm dedicated to world modeling. The world model is formalized as an eight-component cognitive structure comprising entities, relations, canonical predicates, events, causal dependencies, goals, temporal structure, and working memory. Its evolution is governed by a discrete-time world-model operator and a nine-hormone regulatory field combining six hormones inherited from the S-AI corpus with Causine, Temporaline, and Contextine. Nine formal results, WM.0–WM.8, characterize fixed-point existence, convergence, entropy control, coherence safety, computable commitment, finite-time entry into an accepted region, orbit-relative parsimony, and a seven-fold joint guarantee under explicit hypotheses. The implemented source-only action-model pipeline combines ActionParamAgent, PreconditionAgent, EffectAgent, guarded semantic dynamics, structural commit, parse recovery, result-state completion, and precondition anchoring. Experimental results. The final frozen V3.5 pipeline generates and evaluates 101/101 Text2World cases with the official Tarski-based evaluator after pre-GOLD candidate sealing. It reaches 100.00% Executability , 82.997% Levenshtein similarity , 98.008% Predicate F1 , 89.057% Parameter F1 , 60.088% Precondition F1 , and 60.807% Effect F1 . items.summary: Adaptability release: sqzcomb now speaks laboratory units and fits measured data, so the normalized-units engine underneath is usable directly from an experiment. Added sqzcomb.physical : the exact dictionary between laboratory ring parameters and the package's normalized LLE frame. RingSpec (loaded linewidth in Hz, escape efficiency, single-photon Kerr shift, pump wavelength -- with a mandatory reference naming where the numbers come from) plus normalized_pump , threshold_power , normalized_detuning , normalized_dispersion , normalized_frequency / physical_frequency , and intracavity_photons . Conventions are checked by identities rather than trusted: every conversion round-trips exactly, F scales as sqrt(P), and threshold_power is cross-validated through the package's own flat-state cubic -- at the returned power, homogeneous_steady_states contains the rho = 1 root to machine precision. Physical constants come from scipy.constants ; no constant is typed by hand. sqzcomb.fitnoise : extraction of (mu, eta, kappa) from measured homodyne noise spectra in dB relative to shot noise -- the standard characterization of a below-threshold squeezer. fit_noise_spectra fits the package's own input-output model (the same code path as sqzcomb.spectra , cross-checked in the tests against the independent closed form) to the squeezed/antisqueezed trace pair, with an optional white dark-noise floor and per-point measurement sigmas enabling a chi-square consistency check. Identifiability is enforced, not hoped for: one quadrature alone is a single Lorentzian with two shape numbers for three unknowns, so the single-trace fit is refused unless an independently measured kappa_hz is supplied; an antisqueezed trace systematically below shot noise is refused as unphysical. Changed scipy is now a declared dependency (the new modules use scipy.constants and scipy.optimize.least_squares ). Anchors (asserted in tests/test_adapt.py , not stated) Conversion round trips exact to 1e-15; F(4P) = 2F(P); at fixed eta_esc, doubling kappa halves F. threshold_power hits the rho = 1 root of the package's own cubic for alpha in {0.7, 1.0, 1.8}. Noise-free synthetic spectra return the generating (mu, eta, kappa) to better than 1e-6; the fitted model equals the closed form S = 0.5[1 -/+ 4 eta mu / ((1 +/- mu)^2 + Omega^2)] at every frequency to 1e-10. Seeded Monte-Carlo scatter of the fitted parameters matches the reported one-sigma uncertainties; a dark floor deliberately omitted from the model biases eta, and fitting it recovers the truth. The under-determined single-trace case and the impossible below-shot-noise antisqueezed trace are refused with explanatory errors. Full test suite: 80 passed. See CHANGELOG.md for details.

items.summary: We present a synthesis of the Karimov–Alekberli (KA) Framework into a unified theory of Constitutional Intelligence: the capacity of an adaptive system to make consequential decisions that are simultaneously governed, explainable, accountable, reconstructable, verifiable, and capable of learning without retroactive falsification of the historical record. We formulate six formal results — one per required property — organized into three proof tiers: Tier A (two unconditional geometric results), Tier B (three conditional results valid under explicit identifiability and compactness assumptions), Tier C (one KA extension under a physical implementation assumption). Results draw on viability theory,information geometry, and thermodynamics. The theorems are organized in three tiers reflecting their current proof status: Tier A (fully proved geometric results), Tier B (conditional theorems under explicit identifiability and compactness assumptions), and Tier C (KA extensions requiring additional physical or topological conditions). A unifying condition, the Constitutional Integrity Criterion (CIC), is formulated as a representation theorem characterizing systems that satisfy all six properties simultaneously. We derive, under the CIC, that the governance loop Govern → Reason → Act → Remember → Learn → Govern defines a well-defined autonomous map on the constitutional moduli space that preserves the admissible region; fixed-point existence follows as a corollary under compactness. We position the framework within the existing literature on viability theory, formal verification, safe reinforcement learning, AI governance, and constitutional economics. We propose Constitutional Intelligence Science as the emerging discipline that unifies these results.
items.title: Constitutional Intelligence as Formal Science The Karimov–Alekberli Framework as Mathematical Foundation for Governed Institutional Cognition

items.summary: Sanitized code and data reproducibility package for a manuscript currently under double-blind review at the Journal of Information Security and Applications. Author identity is withheld pending the outcome of review. The package contains two independently generated archives: (1) model-I-single-branch/ — a single clock-controlled ternary LFSR generator over GF(3) (controller LFSR A + data LFSR B), together with its exact period and design-condition checkers, a statistical analysis suite, a 14-family ternary long-sequence test battery, and a cryptanalytic attack suite (basic correlation, embedding, fast correlation, Berlekamp-Massey reconstruction, and a linear-consistency/clock-control attack). Includes all 40 archived experiment runs across 8 controller/data degree configurations. (2) model-II-three-branch/ — a three-branch clock-controlled generator over GF(3) combined through a quadratic nonlinear ternary function, together with period/design analysis, algebraic/spectral characterization of the combiner, an aggregate statistical pipeline, avalanche diffusion experiments, a matched attack suite, and an exact key-stream-reuse detector. A full SHA-256 manifest (MANIFEST_SHA256.tsv) and verification script (verify_checksums.py) are included to allow integrity checking of every file. See README.md for directory structure, provenance notes, a documented anonymity sanitization log, and instructions to reproduce all reported results. See CORRESPONDENCE.md for a mapping between source files and the tables/figures of the manuscript. Source code (*.py, *.bat) is released under the MIT License. Generated data, results, logs, CSV aggregates, and figures are released under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).

items.summary: MusiCoMMA connects the Musiconis vocabulary to a bounded pilot of contexts from a pinned CoMMA manuscript-transcription corpus. Its lexical foundation contains 1,198 entries and 1,548 source-sense records. The pilot covers 50 Latin and Old French entries out of 900 in scope. Version 0.2.1 retains 478 contexts across 378 manuscript digitizations after Xavier Fresquet's targeted review of ten chantre windows: three retained and seven excluded. The seven exclusions and all ten decisions are supplied separately. All 485 original annotation assertions remain alongside ten superseding assertions. Source strings and stable identifiers are unchanged. The active set contains 148 automatic links to a single source sense and 330 contexts with unresolved sense assignment. The package includes CSV, JSONL, RDF/Turtle, JSON-LD, schemas, review provenance, an executed Jupyter notebook, analytical tables, figures, checksums and supporting code. A historical baseline archive is included solely for reconstruction. Pilot-dependent analyses have been rerun; unchanged corpus-exposure denominators are reused with checksum provenance. This is a contextual-selection pilot, not an image-verified transcription corpus or a gold-standard benchmark. No independent annotation, corrected readings, population-level precision or recall estimate is claimed. Seven exclusions do not establish seven recognition errors. No manuscript images or bulk CoMMA files are redistributed. Source vocabulary: Musiconis, Sorbonne Université, with explicit credit to Frédéric Billiet and Xavier Fresquet. Source corpus: CoMMA, by Thibault Clérice, Simon Gabay, Malamatenia Vlachou-Efstathiou, Ariane Pinche and Benoît Sagot (2025), HAL hal-05299220v2, https://inria.hal.science/hal-05299220v2. CoMMA-derived material has been extracted, matched, restructured and contextually selected; no institutional endorsement is implied. Data, documentation and analysis outputs: CC BY 4.0. Source-owner authorization for Musiconis and Frédéric Billiet's agreement to deposit were recorded through Xavier Fresquet on 12 September 2026. Linked images remain subject to their providers' conditions.

items.summary: Automated risk decisions increasingly depend on probabilistic assessments transmitted across organisational and computational boundaries. A probability estimate may remain numerically intact while losing the contextual information required to evaluate its evidentiary dependence — a condition we term Provenance Loss . We introduce Orphaned Inference — a probabilistic output P ( H | E ) that propagates downstream after its contextual qualification is stripped at a transmission boundary — and show that when downstream agents continue scalar-posterior updating using marginal likelihood ratios, the resulting propagation is equivalent to a Na ̈ıve-Bayes-style independence approximation over the correlated evidence sequence. This double-counts the shared environmental signal, producing Directional Context Amplification , quantified by the Cumulative Provenance Amplification (CPA n ) metric. Under environmental context drift ( C 0 → C 1 ), accumulated phantom certainty persists into the post-shift regime as Post-Shift Epistemic Persistence , driving the mean absolute posterior error close to 1 in true-negative states ( H = 0) during the pre-shift period. In risk-analysis terms, provenance loss separates the numerical value of a risk estimate from the evidentiary conditions under which it remains decision-valid: downstream decision makers may receive an apparently precise probability whose effective evidentiary weight is substantially overstated. A Monte Carlo simulation ( N = 5 , 000 trials, n = 15 agent chain) demonstrates the predicted cascade under the specified parameter regime and documents monotone growth of CPA n across sampled correlation values ρ ∈ { 0 , . . . , 0 . 8 } . We propose three provenance-aware risk-control safeguards and discuss their governance trade-offs.

items.summary: This record provides the dataset and reproducibility artifact supporting the manuscript “AI-Assisted Security Monitoring in 5G-Enabled UAS Wireless Networks: Run-Wise Validation and Cross-Domain Transfer.” The artifact contains a 17,779-row co-simulation dataset generated from 43 independent 5G/UAS runs, deterministic per-run datasets, scenario manifests, a 44-column telemetry schema, co-simulation and validation code, run-wise machine-learning results, cross-domain transfer results, distribution-shift analyses, manuscript figures, and provenance documentation. items.summary: his work studies the basin geometry of the negative integer Collatz map. Under exact iteration of T(n)={n/2,n even,3n+1,n odd,T(n)= \begin{cases} n/2, & n \text{ even},\\ 3n+1, & n \text{ odd}, \end{cases} the first 10710^7 negative integers are observed to enter one of the three classical negative cycles through −1-1 , −5-5 , and −17-17 . The corresponding empirical basin proportions stabilize near 0.327:0.324:0.3480.327:0.324:0.348 , with a persistent modest excess for the C−17C_{-17} basin. The paper then examines the structure behind these basin frequencies. Basin membership is found to be weakly predicted by simple residue classes modulo 2k2^k , and short prefixes of the 22 -adic valuation itinerary under the accelerated odd Collatz map show essentially no transferable predictive power in held-out tests. A markedly different structure appears in the reverse dynamics. Monotone inverse trees rooted in the three negative attractors show strongly unequal relative sizes, stabilizing near 0.293:0.218:0.4890.293:0.218:0.489 . The associated tree-count ratios remain highly stable over repeated increases in the magnitude cutoff, motivating a common reverse-growth conjecture with basin-dependent amplitudes. Forward trajectories partially erase this reverse-tree asymmetry. Low-reversal trajectories are strongly enriched for the C−17C_{-17} attractor, while increasing non-monotone trajectory complexity attenuates that advantage and moves the observed basin shares closer to the near-balanced global census. The resulting empirical picture is that asymmetric reverse accessibility and forward trajectory mixing jointly shape the macroscopic basin distribution. The paper proposes corresponding conjectures on negative basin densities and reverse-tree ratio convergence. These computations do not prove that every negative integer enters one of the three known cycles, do not exclude additional negative cycles or divergent orbits, and do not resolve the positive Collatz conjecture. The contribution is a computational study of basin structure, reverse accessibility, and mixing in the signed integer extension of the Collatz map.

items.summary: This edition presents the current Split-Zero, theta-cohomology and arithmetic-kernel calculations in a research programme on the Riemann zeta function. It publishes the complete 216-page cumulative continuation, the updated 425-page broader research reader, and their proof sources and checks. The purpose is to make the actual calculations readable and reproducible: what was attempted, why that route was chosen, the maps and estimates obtained, and the precise points where the argument remains unfinished. Start with the cumulative calculation reader 14-splitzero-tau-kernel-continuation.pdf is the primary preview. Its 22 proof sections and nine complete source appendices carry the programme from Split-Zero coefficients through theta cohomology, interpolation kernels, chain retractions, homotopy control and the symmetric arithmetic frontier. Earlier source notes retain their own revisions and attribution; the cumulative continuation is not presented as though all its source results originated in one session. Split-Zero coefficients keep the original zero of a ring as a supported element and adjoin a different, external zero, tau. This records the difference between cancelling a coefficient and forgetting the fibre that carried it. Theta cohomology is a specified space of rapidly decreasing functions modulo the image of a specified theta-summation map. Under the stated Mellin transform, that map becomes multiplication by g(s) = 2 xi(s) , where xi is the completed Riemann zeta function. A finite spectral packet records spectral points with their multiplicities, using polynomial quotients and full derivative data rather than discarding repeated-root directions. The calculations construct minimum-norm representatives from the original arithmetic measure, derive full-jet kernel and Gram-inverse formulas, follow nested packets and tensor constructions, and compute the boundary control from the actual theta-derivative sequence. The cumulative reader also develops the relation-layer graph, derivative quotients, norm and Gram-volume identities, and conjugation/reflection-symmetric estimates. Spectral-sum constructions keep the relative variables through matrix weights and complete nilpotent fibres. The quantitative question is how the control form compares with the original arithmetic Gram matrix as the degree and tensor order grow; smallness of one matrix alone is not treated as the required relative estimate. The broader zeta programme 13-main-reader-425p.pdf supplies the surrounding literature reconstruction, CUE random-matrix calculations, arithmetic transforms and source-directed fluid calculations. It includes the all-axis Mellin calculation, complex axial branch points, moving analytic radius and endpoint-residue map for the stated source patch. Those results are described with their source assumptions and maps; they are not recast as a newly constructed zeta-zero witness or an independent proof of the imported fluid existence result. The motivation includes the use of weights in Deligne's Weil II . This programme works out its own analytic spaces, operators, metrics and comparison maps. The complete proofs retain their domains, signs, measures, scalar actions, local units and multiplicities. These are substantive calculations and research attempts, not a claim that an analogy by itself proves or disproves the Riemann hypothesis. Their manifests pin the exact revisions and file identities. Written analytic arguments, exact finite checks, numerical enclosures and Lean declarations have distinct stated verification scopes; a check on one interface is not promoted into a certificate for the entire programme. items.summary: This record contains the preprint paper "LOST IN THE PDFS: CONTEXT DEGRADATION AND PARAMETRIC HALLUCINATIONS IN LLM UIS" , authored by Gabriele D’Iorio (University of Naples Parthenope).  The study investigates the structural limitations and operational vulnerabilities of commercial web-based Large Language Model (LLM) interfaces when handling long, multi-document sequential workflows in educational contexts. Abstract: The growing use of LLMs for educational purposes, especially by inexperienced users, inevitably leads to LLMs hallucinating and making mistakes. This study presents an experiment using the web version of Gemini (Pro Standard and Flash Standard modes) to simulate a numerical analysis class covering three topics (interpolation, piecewise interpolation, and approximation), each in a separate PDF. This study is subdivided into two scenarios created to evaluate how the LLM responded and, above all, to see how long it took to hallucinate or suffer from context degradation. The results demonstrate the failure of both scenarios due to context degradation. Despite large theoretical context windows, sudden attachment truncation in the web UI forces the model to rely on its parametric memory, leading to severe hallucinations and sycophantic behavior. Key Topics Covered: - Context Degradation & "Lost in the Middle" Phenomenon: Analysis of how LLMs lose retrieval accuracy in prolonged sessions. - Parametric Hallucinations: How models compensate for context loss by fabricating details from pre-training data. - Document Parsing Challenges: Visual layout issues in standard Web UIs. - Experimental Evaluation: A comparative analysis of a single-chat setup (Scenario A) versus a dual-agent/tutor setup (Scenario B). Data Availability: The comprehensive dataset, interaction logs, prompt configurations, and Python scripts used for token counting are openly accessible in the project’s GitHub repository at: https://github.com/gabpolymath/lost_in_the_pdfs/

items.summary: We propose the Encephlian Standard Format (ESF), a 19-channel international 10–20 montage at 250 Hz, average re-referenced, microvolt-calibrated, and channel-wise robust z-scored, as a deterministic canonical representation for deploying pretrained EEG classifiers on heterogeneous acquisition hardware, paired with a recoverability framework that predicts which signal-level shifts ESF can and cannot recover. On the Temple University Abnormal EEG Corpus (TUAB, n = 276 patient-stratified, 253 unique patients), a frozen EEGPT linear probe attains clean AUROC 0.908. We sweep five acquisition-shift axes (native sampling rate, per-channel gain, 50 Hz line noise, electrode montage, and broadband signal-to-noise) and show that left-invertible and bandwidth-preserving operators are (f,0)-recoverable while sub-Nyquist sampling and broadband Gaussian noise are not (Propositions 1, 2). Shift preferentially converts clean normals into confident abnormal reports, the worst direction for screening. items.summary: Generative AI is reshaping how research software is developed. Tools and patterns ranging from “vibe coding” through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and autonomous agents now offer compelling productivity gains, but their adoption in scientific computing surfaces failure modes that general-purpose evaluation does not catch: silent unit conversions, violated conservation laws, hallucinated physics, loss of numerical precision, and quietly broken reproducibility. These failures share a signature: nothing visible goes wrong. The AI ecosystem itself is moving fast, leaving RSEs to make consequential integration decisions with little shared vocabulary or principled guidance. This talk introduces Scientific Agentic Engineering , the central contribution of an in-progress 2026 Better Scientific Software (BSSw) Fellowship: a tool-agnostic methodology for integrating AI agents into high-stakes scientific software workflows. The framework defines how agents, scientific skills, and MCP servers should be structured around validation loops, explicit human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and domain-specific safeguards. Every task moves through a short workflow (frame, plan and critique, implement, verify), with decisions recorded throughout, and the framework maps each documented failure mode to the stage where it is cheapest to catch. The intent is not to recommend any particular AI tool but to articulate foundational concepts that remain valid as the underlying technology changes. I will share three artifacts from the fellowship: The Framework (published July 2026). Shared vocabulary, its principles and workflow, structural guidance on where safeguards live, and a pattern catalog of named practices, each tied to the failure it counters. The Reference Workflow. A structured exercise in which RSEs use AI tools to build a small weather-model error-statistics application, applying the framework to avoid the failure modes it documents. The Community Repository. A curated starter set of scientific MCP server templates, agent skills such as unit checkers and conservation-law validators, and agent configuration examples, designed to be starting points for the community to adapt to a variety of scientific domains. These artifacts are by design community resources, and broader adoption is the explicit aim of the remaining milestones, which include an interactive online tutorial series comparing purpose-built scientific agents with general-purpose tools, a recorded live workshop published for asynchronous access, and a BSSw.io blog post directing the community to the project’s resources. This work engages the conference theme directly by advancing AI-assisted scientific software development from ad-hoc experimentation toward a disciplined, transferable engineering practice.
items.title: Scientific Agentic Engineering: A Framework for Reliable AI Agents in Research Software

items.summary: Adaptability release: sqzcomb now speaks laboratory units and fits measured data, so the normalized-units engine underneath is usable directly from an experiment. Added sqzcomb.physical : the exact dictionary between laboratory ring parameters and the package's normalized LLE frame. RingSpec (loaded linewidth in Hz, escape efficiency, single-photon Kerr shift, pump wavelength -- with a mandatory reference naming where the numbers come from) plus normalized_pump , threshold_power , normalized_detuning , normalized_dispersion , normalized_frequency / physical_frequency , and intracavity_photons . Conventions are checked by identities rather than trusted: every conversion round-trips exactly, F scales as sqrt(P), and threshold_power is cross-validated through the package's own flat-state cubic -- at the returned power, homogeneous_steady_states contains the rho = 1 root to machine precision. Physical constants come from scipy.constants ; no constant is typed by hand. sqzcomb.fitnoise : extraction of (mu, eta, kappa) from measured homodyne noise spectra in dB relative to shot noise -- the standard characterization of a below-threshold squeezer. fit_noise_spectra fits the package's own input-output model (the same code path as sqzcomb.spectra , cross-checked in the tests against the independent closed form) to the squeezed/antisqueezed trace pair, with an optional white dark-noise floor and per-point measurement sigmas enabling a chi-square consistency check. Identifiability is enforced, not hoped for: one quadrature alone is a single Lorentzian with two shape numbers for three unknowns, so the single-trace fit is refused unless an independently measured kappa_hz is supplied; an antisqueezed trace systematically below shot noise is refused as unphysical. Changed scipy is now a declared dependency (the new modules use scipy.constants and scipy.optimize.least_squares ). Anchors (asserted in tests/test_adapt.py , not stated) Conversion round trips exact to 1e-15; F(4P) = 2F(P); at fixed eta_esc, doubling kappa halves F. threshold_power hits the rho = 1 root of the package's own cubic for alpha in {0.7, 1.0, 1.8}. Noise-free synthetic spectra return the generating (mu, eta, kappa) to better than 1e-6; the fitted model equals the closed form S = 0.5[1 -/+ 4 eta mu / ((1 +/- mu)^2 + Omega^2)] at every frequency to 1e-10. Seeded Monte-Carlo scatter of the fitted parameters matches the reported one-sigma uncertainties; a dark floor deliberately omitted from the model biases eta, and fitting it recovers the truth. The under-determined single-trace case and the impossible below-shot-noise antisqueezed trace are refused with explanatory errors. Full test suite: 80 passed. See CHANGELOG.md for details.

items.summary: Doucette rereads Keynes’s 1930 essay “Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren” as a sequencing rule, not a prophecy of mass idleness or automatic leisure. Keynes defined technological unemployment as a pace problem: labor-saving discovery outruns new uses for labor. He called it a temporary maladjustment, while predicting long-run abundance through technical progress and capital accumulation. Doucette applies this framework to the U.S. mid-2020s, focusing on generative AI’s early labor-market effects and the data-center buildout. AI stress appears mainly in junior cognitive work and entry-level hiring, not the national unemployment rate. Data centers are capital-intensive, labor-sparse operations: thousands of construction jobs, few permanent ones, and local conflict over water, power, rates, and consent. They resemble power stations or switching offices more than factories. Northern Virginia illustrates the consent problem. Keynes said little about ownership, so the paper imports distribution: who captures the dividend? It proposes three tests: absorption (rebuild the first rung), cost assignment (large loads pay incremental infrastructure costs), and the dividend (where productivity appears). It considers accelerationist, localist, and leisure-skeptic objections. Limitations include early evidence, mixed data, and one mature cluster. The conclusion separates two clocks: short-run maladjustment and long-run abundance. AI is neither a completed solution nor a surplus of workers; it changes task content and drives physical accumulation. The task is to keep entry paths open, assign costs to the load causing them, and track whether productivity reaches typical pay. Failure would be institutional, not technical.

items.summary: Whether a neural language model can report facts about its own computation is difficult to evaluate because an accurate report may be generated either from the realized runtime state or from a static simulation of the computation conditioned on the input and fixed parameters. We formalize this distinction and show that, under deterministic inference, an internal property of an unperturbed forward pass is not by itself sufficient to distinguish these mechanisms: the realized state is an exact deterministic function of the static input and parameters.  We introduce the Exogenous State Watermark (ESW), a controlled intervention protocol in which an externally sampled perturbation is injected into an intermediate representation while the model's observable next-token output is audited for greedy invariance. For the isolated watermark bit, the static information set has a 50% Bayes-optimal chance bound under the stated independence assumptions. For the counterfactual target, we evaluate unperturbed-state and runtime representations empirically on GPT-2 (124M parameters; width 768). In ESW-1A, a planted directional watermark becomes increasingly decodable as training examples grow relative to representation dimension, reaching 88.4% held-out accuracy at N/d=6.51 (cos θ = 0.9236), while a one-dimensional control reaches 100.0%. In an exploratory Oracle Ladder diagnostic, differential signals peak at Layer 8 before downstream attenuation. In the subsequent multi-seed paired-counterfactual benchmark (ESW-2B), an external nonlinear probe of intermediate runtime differences reaches approximately 0.62–0.63 AUROC, while the tested unperturbed-state baseline remains close to chance (0.507 AUROC) and a sample-label decoupled control remains at 0.546 AUROC. The paired bootstrap difference between the joint and runtime-only models includes zero (ΔAUROC = +0.012, 95% CI [-0.023, +0.047]), demonstrating that adding baseline activations provides no statistically detectable advantage over the runtime perturbation alone.  We interpret the experiments as empirical evidence for runtime-state-dependent decodability under the ESW intervention, not as evidence that GPT-2 possesses autonomous introspection, privileged self-report, consciousness, or subjective self-knowledge.
items.title: Runtime-State Watermarking in Transformers: A Controlled Protocol for Distinguishing Static Self-Simulation from Runtime-State Decodability

items.summary: MusiCoMMA connects the Musiconis vocabulary to a bounded pilot of contexts from a pinned CoMMA manuscript-transcription corpus. Its lexical foundation contains 1,198 entries and 1,548 source-sense records. The pilot covers 50 Latin and Old French entries out of 900 in scope. Version 0.2.1 retains 478 contexts across 378 manuscript digitizations after Xavier Fresquet's targeted review of ten chantre windows: three retained and seven excluded. The seven exclusions and all ten decisions are supplied separately. All 485 original annotation assertions remain alongside ten superseding assertions. Source strings and stable identifiers are unchanged. The active set contains 148 automatic links to a single source sense and 330 contexts with unresolved sense assignment. The package includes CSV, JSONL, RDF/Turtle, JSON-LD, schemas, review provenance, an executed Jupyter notebook, analytical tables, figures, checksums and supporting code. A historical baseline archive is included solely for reconstruction. Pilot-dependent analyses have been rerun; unchanged corpus-exposure denominators are reused with checksum provenance. This is a contextual-selection pilot, not an image-verified transcription corpus or a gold-standard benchmark. items.summary: Whether a neural language model can report facts about its own computation is difficult to evaluate because an accurate report may be generated either from the realized runtime state or from a static simulation of the computation conditioned on the input and fixed parameters. We formalize this distinction and show that, under deterministic inference, an internal property of an unperturbed forward pass is not by itself sufficient to distinguish these mechanisms: the realized state is an exact deterministic function of the static input and parameters.  We introduce the Exogenous State Watermark (ESW), a controlled intervention protocol in which an externally sampled perturbation is injected into an intermediate representation while the model's observable next-token output is audited for greedy invariance. For the isolated watermark bit, the static information set has a 50% Bayes-optimal chance bound under the stated independence assumptions. For the counterfactual target, we evaluate unperturbed-state and runtime representations empirically on GPT-2 (124M parameters; width 768). In ESW-1A, a planted directional watermark becomes increasingly decodable as training examples grow relative to representation dimension, reaching 88.4% held-out accuracy at N/d=6.51 (cos θ = 0.9236), while a one-dimensional control reaches 100.0%. In an exploratory Oracle Ladder diagnostic, differential signals peak at Layer 8 before downstream attenuation. In the subsequent multi-seed paired-counterfactual benchmark (ESW-2B), an external nonlinear probe of intermediate runtime differences reaches approximately 0.62–0.63 AUROC, while the tested unperturbed-state baseline remains close to chance (0.507 AUROC) and a sample-label decoupled control remains at 0.546 AUROC. The paired bootstrap difference between the joint and runtime-only models includes zero (ΔAUROC = +0.012, 95% CI [-0.023, +0.047]), demonstrating that adding baseline activations provides no statistically detectable advantage over the runtime perturbation alone.  We interpret the experiments as empirical evidence for runtime-state-dependent decodability under the ESW intervention, not as evidence that GPT-2 possesses autonomous introspection, privileged self-report, consciousness, or subjective self-knowledge.
items.title: Runtime-State Watermarking in Transformers: A Controlled Protocol for Distinguishing Static Self-Simulation from Runtime-State Decodability

items.summary: This dataset provides a harmonized global collection of river discharge (Q), suspended sediment concentration (SSC), and suspended sediment load (SSL) observations for source-traceable sediment-data analysis and model evaluation. It integrates observations from multiple monitoring networks, regional datasets, literature compilations, and satellite-derived products, with standardized metadata, coordinates, temporal information, variable definitions, and units. Missing sediment variables are derived where appropriate, gauge locations are linked to MERIT-Basins river reaches and upstream drainage units, and variable-level quality flags are provided to distinguish good, derived, suspect, bad, and missing values. Provenance information is preserved so that released records can be traced to their contributing source stations and datasets. The release consists of three complementary components. The main station-reference component contains 7,135 unique stations and 2,997,121 records from 17 source datasets spanning 1912–2025, distributed as separate daily, monthly, and annual station-by-time NetCDF products according to source-reported temporal support. The climatology auxiliary component contains 1,361 stations from five sources and provides long-term or climatological Q, SSC, and SSL information, with reported source coverage extending from 1884 to 2017. The satellite-derived auxiliary component contains 38,550 locations and 16,478,276 records from three source datasets spanning 1984–2020 and provides complementary spatial coverage, mainly for SSC. The archive includes the daily, monthly, and annual NetCDF products; climatology and satellite-derived auxiliary NetCDF products and their accompanying query catalogues; station, source-station, and source-dataset catalogues; and dataset documentation. The catalogues preserve station-level and source-level provenance and support station screening, source tracing, and reproducible use of the released products. The main station-reference component is intended for station-level time-series extraction, source-traceable benchmarking, and evaluation of hydrological, river-routing, erosion, sediment-transport, and land-surface models. The climatology and satellite-derived components provide complementary long-term and spatial context and should not be treated as direct substitutes for the time-resolved station-reference products. Daily, monthly, and annual products represent different temporal support and should be selected according to the requirements of each analysis rather than combined without accounting for observation coverage. This dataset is intended as a reusable and extensible community resource. Future releases may incorporate additional observations and improvements to the harmonization and integration framework while preserving versioned releases for reproducibility.
items.title: A Harmonized Global Station-Reference Dataset of River Discharge, Suspended Sediment Concentration, and Suspended Sediment Load

items.summary: QN-AEI is a curated, simulation-based benchmark for studying quantum noise effects in amplitude-encoded grayscale images. Two hundred images from the BSDS500 training subset were converted to grayscale, resized to 64 x 64 pixels, and encoded as 4096-dimensional normalized amplitude vectors, each corresponding to a 12-qubit quantum state. Every image was then evolved under three completely positive trace-preserving noise channels — amplitude damping, Pauli-Z dephasing, and depolarizing noise — at four channel-parameter values, eta = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7, with 200 repeated stochastic realizations per image-channel-noise configuration. The release therefore contains 2,400 image-channel-noise conditions, 480,000 noisy amplitude-encoded realizations, and 1,966,080,000 normalized perturbation samples. Each image-level record stores the preprocessed clean image, the clean amplitude vector, the noisy statevector matrices, raw and pooled perturbation arrays, normalized bounded-domain perturbation values, and structured condition-level metadata including a deterministic per-condition random seed. The release also includes a dataset manifest, source-image provenance linking every record to its BSDS500 original, an automated validation report covering all 200 records, aggregated and condition-level perturbation statistics, and the MATLAB script used to generate and validate the dataset. The original BSDS500 image files are not redistributed. Users should obtain them from the Berkeley Computer Vision Group and comply with the BSDS500 usage terms. The dataset supports reproducible benchmarking of quantum-noise modeling, bounded-domain perturbation modeling, denoising and error-mitigation methods, and uncertainty and reliability analysis using the repeated realizations. Due to the size of the release (12.6 GB) and Zenodo's current infrastructure load, QN-AEI-BSD200_v1.0.zip is distributed as 26 sequential parts (QN-AEI-BSD200_v1.0.zip.part001 through QN-AEI-BSD200_v1.0.zip.part026) rather than a single file. items.summary: Extraction code, full concordance, both coders' independent judgements and the adjudication record for the article "In Our Lands": Region, Language, and Community in Ibn Sīnā's First Person. Every first-person plural in nineteen works of Ibn Sīnā (2,070,759 words) was extracted and classified, together with three control authors — al-Bīrūnī, Abū Bakr al-Rāzī and al-Fārābī — for a total of fifty-nine works and 410 instances. All instances were coded independently by two readers, the second blind to the hypothesis; the 49 disagreements were adjudicated against written criteria. Both readers' original codes are preserved unaltered. Source texts are from the OpenITI corpus, version 2025.1.9 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17767721); the texts themselves are not redistributed here. See README.md in the archive for a file-by-file description, the coding scheme, headline figures and reproduction instructions. Licence note: data/ is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (inherited from OpenITI via ShareAlike); code/ and protocol/ are MIT. See LICENCE-data.txt and LICENCE-code.txt. The second coding pass was carried out independently, and blind to the hypothesis, by a colleague who has asked not to be named; their codes are included in full as data/codes_reader_B.csv, and the adjudication record in data/uzlastirilmis.csv shows where their reading was preferred.

items.summary: Sanitized code and data reproducibility package for a manuscript currently under double-blind review at the Journal of Information Security and Applications. Author identity is withheld pending the outcome of review. The package contains two independently generated archives: (1) model-I-single-branch/ — a single clock-controlled ternary LFSR generator over GF(3) (controller LFSR A + data LFSR B), together with its exact period and design-condition checkers, a statistical analysis suite, a 14-family ternary long-sequence test battery, and a cryptanalytic attack suite (basic correlation, embedding, fast correlation, Berlekamp-Massey reconstruction, and a linear-consistency/clock-control attack). Includes all 40 archived experiment runs across 8 controller/data degree configurations. (2) model-II-three-branch/ — a three-branch clock-controlled generator over GF(3) combined through a quadratic nonlinear ternary function, together with period/design analysis, algebraic/spectral characterization of the combiner, an aggregate statistical pipeline, avalanche diffusion experiments, a matched attack suite, and an exact key-stream-reuse detector. A full SHA-256 manifest (MANIFEST_SHA256.tsv) and verification script (verify_checksums.py) are included to allow integrity checking of every file. See README.md for directory structure, provenance notes, a documented anonymity sanitization log, and instructions to reproduce all reported results. See CORRESPONDENCE.md for a mapping between source files and the tables/figures of the manuscript. Source code (*.py, *.bat) is released under the MIT License. Generated data, results, logs, CSV aggregates, and figures are released under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).
items.title: Reproducibility package for "Clock-Controlled Ternary Sequence Generators over GF(3): Exact Periods, Statistical Structure, and Cryptanalytic Comparison of Single-Branch and Three-Branch Nonlinear Architectures"
